                                        August 17, 2026

via Electronic Submission
Public Utility Commission of Texas
PUC Docket No. 59475
Bell County East to Big Hill 765-kV Transmission Line Project

       Re: Notice of Proposed Ordering Paragraph in Howard-Solstice Proposal for Decision

Dear Commissioners:
       The Comanche Nation (“Nation”), an Intervenor in Docket No. 59475, hereby advises the
Commissioners of a development that has transpired since the hearing in this matter. Specifically,
on July 27, 2026, the Administrative Law Judges (“ALJ”) in the Howard-Solstice Transmission
Line Project proceeding, SOAH Docket No. 473-26-14355/PUC Docket No. 59336, issued a
Proposal for Decision (“PFD”). Crucially, page 127 of the Howard-Solstice PFD contains a
proposed ordering paragraph that is substantially similar to the Nation’s proposed ordering
paragraphs filed with its reply brief in the instant docket (No. 59475). See Comanche Nation’s
Reply Brief 11-14 (June 26, 2025, Item No. 6339).

       The ALJs’ relevant proposed ordering paragraph from the Howard-Solstice PFD states:

       12. To protect Apache and Comanche tribal and cultural resources, Applicants
       must:

           •   Engage a tribal-approved monitor during initial field surveys and all
               ground-disturbing activities;

           •   Submit an Unanticipated Discovery Plan prior to construction to address
               how the Project will proceed in the event tribal resources are discovered
               during construction. The Unanticipated Discovery Plan should include
               notification protocols for the Comanche and Apache tribes, and require
               coordination with the tribal monitor in assessing cultural discoveries;

           •   When a Marker Tree is identified during cultural resource surveys, halt all
               construction until the Texas Historical Commission and tribal monitor have
               coordinated to complete field verification and document the tree through
               photographs and data collection methods meeting Historic American
               Landscape Survey standards; and

           •   Prior to removing redberry cedar, Pinchot’s juniper, or Texas mountain
               laurel, allow the Comanche Nation to harvest these species used in their
               religious and cultural practices where feasible.
         The Howard-Solstice PFD establishes clear precedent for the cultural resource
protections the Nation seeks in the instant case. A copy of the PFD issued in the Howard-Solstice
Transmission Line Project is attached for your convenience.


                                            Sincerely,


                                            Jennifer S. Baker, OK Bar No. 21938;
                                            NM Bar No. 28101 (pro hac vice in 59475 granted)
                                            PIPESTEM LAW, P.C.
                                            401 S. Boston Avenue, Suite 2200
                                            Tulsa, Oklahoma 74103

I.    INTRODUCTION


      AEP Texas, Inc. (AEP) and the City of San Antonio, acting by and through the
City Public Service Board (CPS Energy) (jointly, Applicants) filed an Application
with the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) to amend their
certificates of convenience and necessity (CCNs) to construct, own, and operate the
 Howard-to-Solstice 765-kilovolt (kV) transmission line in Atascosa, Bandera, Bexar,
Crockett, Edwards, Kerr, Kinney, Medina, Pecos, Real, Sutton, Terrell, Uvalde, and
Val Verde counties (Project).


        The Project is one of five extra-high-voltage transmission lines designated in
the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRB) that was developed by the Electric
Reliability Council ofTexas (ERCOT) and approved by the Commission.1 The PBRP
identified a need for additional transmission capacity to serve forecasted electrical
load in the Permian Basin region, where load growth is being driven by oil and gas
development, data centers, crypto-mining, and other types of large loads.2 ERCOT
proposed a number of transmission projects to meet this identified need, and after
approving the PBRP, the Commission proceeded to authorize transmission service
providers (TSPs), including AEP and CPS Energy, to move forward with seeking
CCN authorization for five transmission lines on three 765-kV import paths intended
to transfer power from other regions of the state into the Permian Basin region.3
These will be the first 765-kV lines constructed in the state of Texas. AEP and
CPS Energy were assigned responsibility to construct, own, and operate Import
Path 3, the Project at issue in this proceeding.

             The Project will begin at CPS Energy's existing Howard Station, which is
located in the southwest San Antonio area, and extend west-northwest until it
reaches AEP's existing Solstice Station, which is located approximately 28 miles west
of Fort Stockton.4 The Howard and Solstice substations are currently 345-kV
stations but will be expanded for 765-kV operation.5 Applicants have agreed to divide
ownership of the new 765-kV transmission line, with CPS Energy owning the eastern
half of the line, beginning at its Howard substation, and AEP owning the western half
beginning at its Solstice substation. Applicants will each be responsible for design,
right-of-way (ROW) acquisition, material procurement, and construction on their
respective portions of the line.6 The Project also includes telecommunication
facilities (including necessary fiber repeater huts) that are critical to the reliable
operation ofthe proposed transmission line facilities.7

approximately 335 to 393 miles long, depending on the route selected. The estimated

II.     JURISDICTION AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY


         A.      JURISDICTION AND DEADLINE


         The Commission has jurisdiction and authority over the Application under
Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA)10 sections 14.001, 32.001, 37.051, .053, and
.056, and 16 Texas Administrative Code § (Rule) 25.101. SOAH has jurisdiction to
conduct a hearing and render a proposal for decision (PFD) on the Application under
PURA section 14.053 and Texas Government Code section 2003.049.


         This docket was opened on February 6,2026, and the Application was filed
on March 2,2026. This case is subject to a 180-day deadline established in PURA
section 37.057, which requires the Commission to issue a final order on a CCN
application not later than the 180th day after the application was filed, and does not

the prehearing conference on March 26, then adopted a procedural schedule in
SOAH Order No. 4, issued on March 30,2026.

         On May 19-22, 2026, SOAH ALJs Starnes and Davis held a hybrid hearing,
where parties and witnesses could attend by videoconference or in person. Most of
the intervenors elected to attend remotely, particularly those who were
self-represented, but roughly 80 attorneys and their witnesses preferred to attend in
person. Because the number of people slated to attend in person exceeded the
capacity of SOAH's hearing facilities, the in-person portion of the hearing convened
in a conference room at the Hilton Austin Airport Hotel in Austin, Texas, a facility
arranged by Applicants.


        At the time of the hearing, approximately 230 intervenors remained parties.25
Nearly 400 exhibits from approximately 80 separate parties were admitted into
evidence, including testimony from 147 individual witnesses. Approximately
55 intervenors or aligned groups of intervenors actively participated in the hearing,
during which 22 witnesses were cross-examined. Following the hearing, the parties'
written closing arguments and any offers ofproofwere due on May 27,2026. Replies
to written closing arguments were due on June 1, 2026, and the record closed on that
date.


        C.      INTERVENORS'DUE PROCESS CONCERNS

 III.    APPLICABLE LAW


        In considering a CCN application for new transmission facilities, the
Commission may take one of three actions: grant the certificate as requested, grant
the certificate for a portion of the facilities, or refuse to grant the certificate.41 The
Commission may approve an application and grant or amend a CCN only if the
facilities are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the
public.42 Additionally, the Commission must consider the following statutory and
regulatory factors:43
         1.      the adequacy of existing service;

        2.       the need for additional service;

        3.       the effect of granting the certificate on the recipient of the certificate
                 and any electric utility serving the proximate area; and

        4.       other factors, such as:

                 a.       community values;

                 b.       recreational and park areas;

                 c.       historical and aesthetic values;

                 d.       environmental integrity;

                 e.       the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to
                          consumers in the area if the certificate is granted;

                 f.       the need for extending transmission service where existing or
                          projected electrical loads will be underserved, including where:

42 PURA § 37.056(a); see also 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b).

                          (ii)     the available capacity is unreasonably limited at
                                   transmission or distribution voltage level; or

                          (iii)    the electrical load cannot be interconnected in a timely
                                   manner;

                 g.       engineering constraints;

                 h.       costs;

                 i.       to the extent reasonable, whether the impact of the line on the
                          affected community and landowners can be moderated;

                 j.       whether the routes parallel or utilize existing compatible ROW
                          for electric facilities;

                 k.       whether the routes parallel or utilize other existing compatible

                          ROW;

                 1.       whether the routes parallel property lines or other natural or

                 m.       whether the routes conform with the policy of prudent

        Some of the factors are inherently in conflict, and neither PURA nor
Commission rules specify the relative weight to be given to each factor. For example,
some factors favor the paralleling of roads and maintaining environmental integrity,
which could lead to the conclusion that transmission lines should be placed along
roadways and avoid bisecting undeveloped land. However, the factors also favor
moderating the impact to the community and consideration of community values

reasonable investments of money and effort." 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(a)(6).

 (which, as in this case, often includes maximizing the distance from the proposed line
to residences). Consideration of these factors could lead to the conclusion that the
line should be placed as far from residences as possible. The Commission and the
Aus have the difficult task of considering the totality of all factors, even ifindividual
factors, when considered in isolation, could lead to opposite outcomes. The Texas
Third Court of Appeals recognized this challenge when it held: "None of the
statutory factors is intended to be absolute in the sense that any one shall prevail in
all possible circumstances. In making these sometimes-delicate accommodations, the
agency is required to exercise its ' expertise ' to further the overall public interest . 3 ) 45

            Impacts on Surface and Groundwater.215 The study area overlies five major
aquifers-the Carrizo Wilcox, Edwards (Balcones Fault Zone), Edwards Trinity
(Plateau), Trinity, and Pecos Valley. The Carrizo Wilcox Aquifer occupies the
easternmost portion and consists of thick sand formations used for irrigation and
municipal supply. West of it, the Edwards (Balcones Fault Zone) Aquifer is a highly
permeable limestone system feeding major springs such as Comal and San Marcos.
The Edwards Trinity (Plateau) Aquifer underlies much ofthe central study area, with
generally fresh water used for irrigation, municipal, and livestock supply. The Trinity
Aquifer lies farther west and consists of multiple smaller aquifers within the Trinity
Group, supporting municipal, irrigation, livestock, and domestic uses. The Pecos
Valley Aquifer underlies the extreme westernmost portion of the study area and is
composed of alluvial and windblown deposits filling structural basins such as the
Pecos Trough. Its water quality varies and may contain elevated chloride, sulfate,
arsenic, and radionuclides; it primarily supports irrigation, with additional
municipal, industrial, and power generation uses. Numerous private and public water
wells and natural springs occur throughout the study area.


           The study area spans all three Edwards Aquifer zones-Contributing,
Recharge, and Artesian-where rainfall moves from the Edwards Plateau into
fractured limestone recharge features and then into confined artesian units. It lies
within the jurisdictional areas of Edwards Aquifer Authority (EAA) Districts 4,5,6,
7, 12, 13, 14, and 15, with EAA regulatory authority in Atascosa, Bexar, Medina, and
Uvalde counties. The EAA regulates groundwater withdrawals and may regulate

I.    INTRODUCTION


      AEP Texas, Inc. (AEP) and the City of San Antonio, acting by and through the
City Public Service Board (CPS Energy) (jointly, Applicants) filed an Application
with the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) to amend their
certificates of convenience and necessity (CCNs) to construct, own, and operate the
 Howard-to-Solstice 765-kilovolt (kV) transmission line in Atascosa, Bandera, Bexar,
Crockett, Edwards, Kerr, Kinney, Medina, Pecos, Real, Sutton, Terrell, Uvalde, and
Val Verde counties (Project).


         The Project is one of five extra-high-voltage transmission lines designated in
the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRB) that was developed by the Electric
Reliability Council ofTexas (ERCOT) and approved bythe Commission.1 The PBRP
identified a need for additional transmission capacity to serve forecasted electrical
load in the Permian Basin region, where load growth is being driven by oil and gas
development, data centers, crypto-mining, and other types of large loads.2 ERCOT
proposed a number of transmission projects to meet this identified need, and after
approving the PBRP, the Commission proceeded to authorize transmission service
providers (TSPs), including AEP and CPS Energy, to move forward with seeking
CCN authorization for five transmission lines on three 765-kV import paths intended
to transfer power from other regions of the state into the Permian Basin region.3
These will be the first 765-kV lines constructed in the state of Texas. AEP and
CPS Energy were assigned responsibility to construct, own, and operate Import
Path 3, the Project at issue in this proceeding.

 III.       APPLICABLE LAW


           In considering a CCN application for new transmission facilities, the
Commission may take one of three actions: grant the certificate as requested, grant
the certificate for a portion of the facilities, or refuse to grant the certificate.41 The
Commission may approve an application and grant or amend a CCN only if the
facilities are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the
public.42 Additionally, the Commission must consider the following statutory and
regulatory factors:43
           1.       the adequacy of existing service;

           2.       the need for additional service;

           3.       the effect of granting the certificate on the recipient of the certificate
                    and any electric utility serving the proximate area; and

           4.       other factors, such as:
                    a.       community values;

                    b.      recreational and park areas;
                    c.      historical and aesthetic values;

                    d.       environmental integrity;

                    e.      the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to
                            consumers in the area if the certificate is granted;

                    f.      the need for extending transmission service where existing or
                            projected electrical loads will be underserved, including where:

        Some of the factors are inherently in conflict, and neither PURA nor
Commission rules specify the relative weight to be given to each factor. For example,
some factors favor the paralleling of roads and maintaining environmental integrity,
which could lead to the conclusion that transmission lines should be placed along
roadways and avoid bisecting undeveloped land. However, the factors also favor
moderating the impact to the community and consideration of community values

 (which, as in this case, often includes maximizing the distance from the proposed line
to residences). Consideration of these factors could lead to the conclusion that the
line should be placed as far from residences as possible. The Commission and the
ALJs have the difficult task of considering the totality of all factors, even if individual
factors, when considered in isolation, could lead to opposite outcomes. The Texas
Third Court of Appeals recognized this challenge when it held: "None of the
statutory factors is intended to be absolute in the sense that any one shall prevail in
all possible circumstances. In making these sometimes-delicate accommodations, the
agency is required to exercise its ' expertise ' to further the overall public interest . 33 45

            Impacts on Surface and Groundwater. 215 The study area overlies five major
aquifers-the Carrizo Wilcox, Edwards (Balcones Fault Zone), Edwards Trinity
(Plateau), Trinity, and Pecos Valley. The Carrizo Wilcox Aquifer occupies the
easternmost portion and consists of thick sand formations used for irrigation and
municipal supply. West of it, the Edwards (Balcones Fault Zone) Aquifer is a highly
permeable limestone system feeding major springs such as Comal and San Marcos.
The Edwards Trinity (Plateau) Aquifer underlies much ofthe central study area, with
generally fresh water used for irrigation, municipal, and livestock supply. The Trinity
Aquifer lies farther west and consists of multiple smaller aquifers within the Trinity
Group, supporting municipal, irrigation, livestock, and domestic uses. The Pecos
Valley Aquifer underlies the extreme westernmost portion of the study area and is
composed of alluvial and windblown deposits filling structural basins such as the
Pecos Trough. Its water quality varies and may contain elevated chloride, sulfate,
arsenic, and radionuclides; it primarily supports irrigation, with additional
municipal, industrial, and power generationuses. Numerous private and public water
wells and natural springs occur throughout the study area.


           The study area spans all three Edwards Aquifer zones-Contributing,
Recharge, and Artesian-where rainfall moves from the Edwards Plateau into
fractured limestone recharge features and then into confined artesian units. It lies
within the jurisdictional areas of Edwards Aquifer Authority (EAA) Districts 4,5,6,
7, 12, 13, 14, and 15, with EAA regulatory authority in Atascosa, Bexar, Medina, and
Uvalde counties. The EAA regulates groundwater withdrawals and may regulate
